claims.claim: The two source-stated bounds imply total update time Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}). This meets Õ(n√m) when m≤n^(6/5) and when m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n; over all m it is within an Õ(n^(1/4)) factor of the target.
claims.evidence: Relative to n√m, the sparse and dense bounds have ratios m^(5/6)/n and n/√m. The first is at most one exactly for m≤n^(6/5); the second is polylogarithmic when m≥n²/log^C n. Their envelope is maximized where m^(4/3)=n², namely m=n^(3/2), and the ratio there is n^(1/4).
claims.witness: For m=n^(3/2), both available bounds equal n² while n√m=n^(7/4), realizing the n^(1/4) polynomial gap.
claims.search_method: Symbolic exponent comparison, including monotonicity on both sides of the crossover, corroborated with exact rational arithmetic.

claims.claim: Reachability-rectangle identity: if R is reflexive reachability immediately before inserting u→v, A={x:xRu}, D={y:vRy}, and R⁺ is reachability afterward, then R⁺=R∪(A×D). Hence an insertion sequence evolves reachability exactly by monotone union with these time-dependent ancestor–descendant rectangles.
claims.evidence: Any newly reachable x-to-y pair has a simple post-insertion path using u→v exactly once, whose prefix and suffix are old paths, so xRu and vRy. Conversely those two old paths concatenate with u→v. Old reachability persists, proving both inclusions even if the old graph is cyclic.
claims.witness: A new pair (x,y) factors as x R u, then u→v, then v R y; this is precisely membership in A×D.
claims.search_method: Direct two-inclusion proof and exhaustive testing of every loop-free directed graph on four vertices with every missing directed insertion.

claims.claim: Corrected balanced-cut lemma: for every order-violating insertion u→v into a DAG, either v already reaches u, so the insertion closes a cycle, or one can find equally sized sets B,F and a cut c such that F consists of the descendants of v at or left of c, B consists of the ancestors of u right of c, the stable order (L\F),B,F,(R\B) is topological after the insertion, and all |B||F| ordered pairs in B×F become newly reachable.
claims.evidence: In the acyclic branch, the descendant set D(v) and ancestor set A(u) are disjoint. Sweeping a cut from before v to before u, h=|D∩L|−|A∩R| starts negative, ends nonnegative, and changes only by zero or one, so it attains zero with positive common size. The only old-edge inversions introduced by the stable reorder are F→(L\F), (R\B)→B, or F→B; descendant closure, ancestor closure, and absence of a v-to-u path respectively exclude them. The new u→v edge is forward. Every b∈B reaches every f∈F afterward, while the old topological order placed f before b, proving freshness.
claims.witness: At a zero of h, take F=D(v)∩L and B=A(u)∩R. Then u∈B, v∈F, |B|=|F|>0, and B×F supplies |B||F| distinct new proper reachability pairs.
claims.search_method: Symbolic sweep and inversion-case proof, plus exhaustive checking of every DAG compatible with a fixed six-vertex topological order and every acyclic backward insertion.

claims.claim: Structural reduction for the balanced-cut route: suppose a combinatorial ordered-reachability boundary oracle can absorb all edge insertions and stable block reorders in total Õ(n+m+Σ_i q_i) time, and on each violating insertion either reports an old v-to-u path or returns a cut c with F=D(v)∩L_c, B=A(u)∩R_c, and |B|=|F|=q_i>0. Then it yields an incremental topological-sort algorithm with total update time Õ(n√m).
claims.evidence: The balanced-cut lemma makes every returned reorder topological. Its q_i² pairs are newly reachable, so rectangles charged at different updates are disjoint and Σq_i²≤n(n−1). With at most m such updates, Cauchy–Schwarz gives (Σq_i)²≤mΣq_i²=O(mn²), hence Σq_i=O(n√m). A sequence tree adds only soft-O(Σq_i), and for 1≤m≤n² the assumed n+m term is O(n√m).
claims.witness: The decisive charge is Σ_i q_i²≤n(n−1), followed by Σ_i q_i≤√(mΣ_i q_i²)=O(n√m).
claims.search_method: Checked the conditional interface against the balanced-cut invariant and audited every additive term; exact small-sequence checks corroborated the charging inequality.

claims.claim: The balanced-cut construction gives an explicit combinatorial algorithm with total time Õ(m+n√m+A), where A is the total number of adjacency entries scanned from selected forward vertices and selected backward vertices. Consequently it attains Õ(n√m) whenever A=Õ(n√m), including sequences in which every selected forward vertex has polylogarithmic out-degree and every selected backward vertex has polylogarithmic in-degree at its expansion time.
claims.evidence: A min-position forward heap and max-position backward heap enumerate descendants of v and ancestors of u in topological order. Expanding one from each side preserves equal selected-set sizes; an intersection certifies a v-to-u path, while crossed remaining frontiers determine an exact balanced cut. Each successful update expands q_i vertices per side, heap insertions are charged to scanned entries, and stable sequence-tree extraction costs soft-O(q_i). Thus the total is soft-O(m+Σq_i+A), plus at most O(n) work for a terminal cycle search; Claim 3 bounds Σq_i by O(n√m). If every expanded vertex has the stated directional polylogarithmic degree, A is soft-O(Σq_i+n), giving the claimed special case.
claims.witness: In an acyclic search, after q paired expansions the selected vertices are the first q descendants and last q ancestors. When the next descendant lies after the next ancestor, a cut between the two frontiers has exactly those selected sets.
claims.search_method: Invariant and cost audit of the described heap-and-adjacency implementation, with exhaustive finite simulation of frontier crossing, exact cuts, and reordered topological validity.

claims.claim: The rectangle reformulation cannot be implemented by eagerly materializing every newly reachable pair within the target bound: there is an insertion sequence with n=2r and m=2r−1 whose final insertion creates exactly r² new reachability pairs. Thus any implementation doing Ω(1) work per newly created pair takes Ω(n²), not Õ(n√m), on this sequence.
claims.evidence: Two disjoint r-vertex chains use 2r−2 edges. Inserting the edge from the first chain's sink to the second chain's source adds exactly every ordered cross pair from the first chain to the second, and no others, for r² new pairs. Here n√m=Θ(r^(3/2)), whereas per-pair work is Ω(r²), a polynomially larger cost.
claims.witness: The explicit sequence x₁→⋯→x_r, y₁→⋯→y_r, followed by x_r→y₁ has n=2r, m=2r−1, and fresh rectangle {x₁,…,x_r}×{y₁,…,y_r}.
claims.search_method: Direct transitive-closure calculation and exact simulation for r=2 through 8.

claims.claim: Full adjacency-list rescanning cannot be charged automatically to the balanced-search vertex bound: there is a DAG sequence with n=2r+2 and m=4r in which every violating update has q=1 and creates exactly one new reachability pair, yet rescanning the selected forward list costs r².
claims.evidence: With initial edges v→w_j, z→w_j, and u_i→z, insertion u_i→v moves u_i immediately before v. At that moment D(v)∩L={v} and A(u_i)∩R={u_i}, so q=1. Since u_i already reaches every w_j through z, only (u_i,v) is newly reachable. Nevertheless expanding v scans its unchanged r-entry outgoing list on each of r updates, totaling r² scans. The graph remains acyclic and the counts are n=2r+2 and m=3r+r=4r.
claims.witness: The maintained orders are u₁,…,u_(i−1),v,u_i,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r immediately before update i.
claims.search_method: Stepwise order, closure, edge-count, and scan-count verification, including exact simulation for r=2 through 8.

claims.claim: Semantically, the balanced search may be restricted to the old topological interval [v,u]: ignoring forward neighbors after u and backward neighbors before v preserves cycle detection and produces the same descendant/ancestor intersections needed by every cut between v and u.
claims.evidence: Positions strictly increase along every nontrivial old-DAG path. Therefore every v-to-u path lies wholly in [v,u]. Likewise, a path from v to a vertex at or left of an intervening cut cannot visit a vertex after u, and a path from a vertex right of the cut to u cannot visit a vertex before v. The restricted searches consequently preserve both cycle detection and every required D(v)∩L_c and A(u)∩R_c intersection.
claims.witness: For v≤y≤c<u, every vertex on a v-to-y path has position between v and y; the ancestor statement is the reversed argument for c<x≤u.
claims.search_method: Monotonic-position proof and exhaustive interval-versus-full-search comparison on all fixed-order six-vertex DAGs.

claims.claim: Even perfect filtering of adjacency entries outside the active interval does not make full-list balanced expansion Õ(n√m): for every p,q≥2 there is a block-swap sequence on n=pq vertices and m=[pq(q−1)+p(p−1)]/2 edges with p(p−1)/2 violating updates, each having |B|=|F|=q, whose selected-block internal entries alone are rescanned p(p−1)q(q−1)/2 times. Setting p=q² gives m=Θ(n^(4/3)) and Θ(n²) scans, a Θ(n^(1/3)) factor above n√m.
claims.evidence: Inductively, before update (j,a), blocks C_a and C_j are adjacent in that order. The edge from C_j's sink to C_a's source is acyclic and swaps them. At their boundary, the relevant descendant and ancestor intersections are exactly C_a and C_j, so both have size q and the q² pairs C_j×C_a are fresh. Each update scans q(q−1)/2 internal outgoing entries in C_a and the same number of internal incoming entries in C_j. Multiplication by p(p−1)/2 updates gives the stated scan count. For p=q², n=q³, m=q⁴−(q³+q²)/2=Θ(q⁴), scans are Θ(q⁶), and n√m=Θ(q⁵).
claims.witness: The update schedule j=1,…,p−1 and a=0,…,j−1 reverses each processed prefix and processes every unordered block pair exactly once.
claims.search_method: Symbolic block-order induction and exact graph simulation for multiple p,q values, including p=q².

target_evidence: The source requests an unconditional combinatorial soft-O(n√m) incremental topological-sort algorithm. The draft explicitly leaves the required arbitrary-degree ordered-boundary oracle unconstructed, and its concrete implementation retains an uncontrolled scan term A. It therefore does not prove the full target. Nevertheless, the verified balanced-cut lemma, conditional reduction, restricted-degree algorithm, interval restriction, and obstruction families constitute correct material partial progress without claiming unconditional coverage.
